newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean newspapers dismayed by Japan summit.
newsitem.headline: South Korean newspapers dismayed by Japan summit.

text.p: South Korean newspapers and commentators expressed dismay on Sunday at a summit between President Kim Young-sam and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, saying it had failed to heal old wounds.
Newspapers faulted the meeting for treading lightly over the most nettlesome issues between the Asian neighbours, including a territorial dispute and the issue of Japanese wartime sex slaves.
And there was scepticism over Hashimoto's apology for inflamatory comments made by his chief spokesman about the "comfort women" who serviced Japanese front-line troops.
"It is regrettable that issues from the past, such as 'comfort women' and Tokto, were avoided in the summit," said an editorial in the Hankook Ilbo newspaper.
Tokto refers to a group of disputed islands, known in Japanese as Takeshima, surrounded by rich fishing grounds.
"We cannot solve problems by closing our eyes no matter delicate they are. It could invite a bigger disaster later," the newspaper said.
Hashimoto and Kim met on Saturday in the Japanese hot springs resort of Beppu.

Kim Young-ho, a professor of economics at Kyungbuk University, writing in a commentary in the Chosun Ilbo daily, said Japanese conservatives despised a mood of repentance among some of their fellow countrymen for wartime atrocities.
"Hashimoto himself seems to belong to Japan's conservatives," he wrote.
On the eve of the summit, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama indirectly defended the use of the "comfort women" by saying there was a "social background" to the prostitution.
About 200,000 captured "comfort women" from Korea, the Philippines, China, Indonesia and the Netherlands were forced to work in brothels for the Japanese imperial army.
Earlier this month, public anger among Koreans erupted when the Asian Women's Fund, a private group set up in 1995 with Japanese initiative, paid money in compensation to seven ageing Korean women.
Many South Koreans want the Japanese government to pay in an acknowledgement of guilt and repentance.
"Japan should not try to play down the issue by seeking a private solution," said Shin Ki-ha, a history professor at Seoul National University.
But the Hankook Ilbo newspaper praised an agreement on joint efforts to stop Taiwan from shipping nuclear waste to impoverished North Korea.
"The cooperation has made Taiwan's act an object for international outrage," the paper said.
Hashimoto told Kim he shared South Korea's concern that a shipment of 60,000 barrels of nuclear waste to North Korea could have an environmental impact.
